prompts.literature.retell.short: Help me briefly retell a chapter: [my notes or an excerpt]
prompts.literature.retell.detailed: I've read [work and chapter]. Here are my notes on what happens: [notes]. Help me turn them into an 8–10 sentence retelling: in order of events, with the main characters, without minor details. If something's missing for it to make sense, ask me rather than inventing it.
prompts.literature.retell.refine: Shorten the retelling to 3 sentences: only what's needed to follow the next chapter.
prompts.literature.retell.check: Ask 5 questions about the chapter to check how closely I read. Judge my answers against my notes.
prompts.literature.character.detailed: Help me build a character analysis of [character] from “[work]”. Outline: role in the plot, appearance and speech (if relevant), personality traits with the episodes that show them, how the character changes, the author's attitude. Leave gaps for episodes where I'll add examples from the text myself.
prompts.literature.character.refine: Why might the character have acted that way in [episode]? Suggest 2–3 possible explanations.
prompts.literature.character.check: Here's my character analysis: [text]. Where am I describing the character without evidence from the text?
prompts.literature.conflict.detailed: Help me describe the conflict in “[work]”. Cover: who or what it's between (character vs character, character vs society, internal), its cause, how it develops (set-up, climax, resolution), how it ends, what the author wanted to show. If you're unsure about plot details, ask me.
prompts.literature.conflict.refine: Is there a second, less obvious conflict? How does it relate to the main one?
prompts.literature.conflict.check: I think the climax is [episode]. Do you agree? Explain why or why not.
prompts.literature.theme.short: What's the difference between theme and main idea? Show it using “[work]”.
prompts.literature.theme.detailed: Help me identify the theme and main idea of “[work]”. First explain the difference in one sentence. Then suggest 2–3 possible wordings for each and name the episodes that support them. Say which is most accurate and why.
prompts.literature.theme.refine: Connect the work's main idea to today: where is it relevant now?
prompts.literature.theme.check: My wording of the main idea: [wording]. Is it specific enough, or would it fit any book?
prompts.literature.arguments.short: Find arguments for the thesis: [thesis] based on “[work]”.
prompts.literature.arguments.detailed: My thesis: [thesis]. Work: “[work]”. Suggest 3 arguments: for each, the point, which episode could support it, and how to link it back to the thesis. Add 1 counter-argument worth addressing. If you're not sure an episode is in the book, write “check”.
prompts.literature.arguments.refine: Argument [number] is weak. How can I strengthen or replace it?
prompts.literature.arguments.check: Here's my argument paragraph: [paragraph]. Does it have a claim, an example and a conclusion?
prompts.literature.essay.detailed: Make an outline for an essay on “[topic]” based on “[work]”, length [words] words. Structure: introduction with a thesis, 2–3 body parts each with an argument and a hint on which episode to use, a conclusion that answers the question. Don't write finished sentences, just points.
prompts.literature.essay.refine: Suggest 3 different ways to open the essay, without finished text: just the idea of each.
prompts.literature.essay.check: Here's my draft: [draft]. Mark where it drifts off topic and where it needs evidence from the text. Don't rewrite it.
prompts.literature.heroes.detailed: Compare [character 1] and [character 2] from “[work]”. Table: background and position, goals, personality traits, key action, how they change, the author's attitude. Below the table: the main similarity and main difference, and why the author probably placed them side by side.
prompts.literature.heroes.refine: How would each character act in the situation [situation]? Justify it through their personalities.
prompts.literature.heroes.check: Ask me 4 “who is this about?” questions using details from the table, and I'll answer.
prompts.literature.words.short: Explain unfamiliar words from the text: [words]
prompts.literature.words.detailed: I'm reading “[work]” and came across unfamiliar words: [words]. Here are the sentences they're in: [sentences]. Table: word, its meaning in this sentence, a modern synonym, whether it's archaic. If the meaning in context is ambiguous, give options.
prompts.literature.words.refine: What do these words say about the period or the character who uses them?
prompts.literature.words.check: I'll write my own sentences with these words: [sentences]. Have I used them correctly?
prompts.literature.discussion.detailed: Write discussion questions on “[work]” for [class, group or club]: 3 on understanding the plot, 3 on the characters' motives, 2 linking to life today, 1 provocative. No yes-or-no questions. For each, add which episode to draw on.
prompts.literature.discussion.refine: Which questions would spark the liveliest debate? Suggest how to split the group into sides.
prompts.literature.discussion.check: Here's my answer to question [number]: [answer]. Ask me a follow-up question as a discussion partner would.
prompts.literature.quote.detailed: Analyse a quotation from “[work]”: [quotation]. Who says it and when (as I've noted: [context]), its literal meaning, the deeper meaning, the literary devices used, how it connects to the work's theme. Rely on my context notes; don't invent plot.
prompts.literature.quote.refine: How could I use this quotation in an essay on [topic]? Suggest which thesis it would support.
prompts.literature.quote.check: Here's my analysis of the quotation: [analysis]. What have I explained only superficially?

verify.literature.retell: AI can mix up events or characters, especially in lesser-known books. A summary doesn't replace reading: check it against the text.
verify.literature.character: Rely on episodes from the text. If the AI quotes the book, find the quote yourself: it may invent it.
verify.literature.conflict: The conflict can be read in different ways. Compare with how your textbook and teacher interpret it.
verify.literature.theme: Themes and ideas can be worded in many ways. What matters is that yours is grounded in the text, not that it matches someone else's word for word.
verify.literature.arguments: Check every argument against the text: find the page or episode. Arguments not grounded in the text won't count in an exam.
verify.literature.essay: The outline helps, but write the essay yourself: teachers notice AI-written text, and learning to write matters for you.
verify.literature.heroes: Check each row of the table against the text: AI may give one character another's traits or actions.
verify.literature.words: A word's meaning depends on period and context. For old or dialect words, check a dictionary or the notes in your edition.
verify.literature.discussion: Good discussion questions don't have one right answer. Remove any that can be answered with yes or no.
verify.literature.quote: Check the quotation in the book: word for word and with the right author. A misquote undermines the whole answer.
